title: Marketplace FDI review revives the seller-restructuring scramble
dek: Renewed scrutiny of inventory-model breaches has large e-commerce platforms redrawing seller structures, and smaller vendors are caught in the churn.

body.text: Every few years the same set of legal opinions is pulled out of the drawer in the offices of India's largest online marketplaces. This is one of those years. Officials at the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade have been working through a fresh batch of complaints from trader associations alleging that foreign-funded platforms still exercise effective control over inventory they are not permitted to own, and platform counsel have quietly begun another round of defensive restructuring.

The rules have not changed. Press Note 2 of 2018 still allows 100 per cent foreign direct investment in the marketplace model, where the platform is a neutral venue connecting buyers and sellers, and bars it in the inventory model, where the platform owns the goods. What has changed is the level of forensic detail officials are willing to go into. The current examination reaches past equity holdings in seller entities into warehousing agreements, exclusive launch windows, advertising rebates and the commercial terms under which a small number of vendors account for a disproportionate share of a category's sales.

For sellers the consequences are immediate and unglamorous. GST registrations are moved, invoicing entities are renamed, listings are reassigned, and category teams spend weeks reconciling stock that has not physically moved a metre.
The complaint file keeps growing

Trader bodies have been filing versions of the same grievance since the marketplace rules were tightened. The argument is structural rather than anecdotal: if a platform decides which sellers get space in its fulfilment centres, funds their working capital through a lending affiliate, sets their discount participation and then ranks them at the top of search results, the seller's independence is a paper fact. Enforcement agencies have historically found this hard to act on because each individual arrangement, taken alone, is commercially defensible.

The Competition Commission of India's market study on e-commerce, and the investigations that followed it, moved the conversation from ownership to conduct. Deep discounting, preferential listing and exclusive smartphone launches were examined not as FDI breaches but as competition questions. That has left platforms managing two regulators with overlapping interests and different remedies: DPIIT can question the corporate structure, the CCI can question the behaviour, and neither outcome is cheap.

"The FDI test asks who owns the stock and the competition test asks who controls the price, and in practice the same set of contracts answers both," said a partner at a Delhi law firm that advises two large platforms.
Restructuring, again

The standard response is well rehearsed. Seller entities in which the platform or its affiliates hold equity are diluted below the threshold that attracts scrutiny. Warehouse leases are shifted to third-party logistics firms. Category exclusivity is replaced with softer commitments that are harder to characterise as control.

Executives describe the work as expensive and largely cosmetic. One restructuring exercise at a large horizontal platform involved unwinding seller relationships across roughly a dozen categories, a process that took the better part of two quarters and required renegotiating fulfilment terms with vendors who had no interest in changing anything. Volumes dipped during the transition and recovered within a quarter, which is the pattern insiders now expect.

The deeper problem is that the marketplace model, as written, assumes a seller ecosystem with independent capital and independent logistics. Large parts of Indian online retail do not work that way. Sellers on a platform's fulfilment network get faster delivery promises and better conversion, so they concentrate there, and concentration is exactly what regulators read as control.
Where the cost lands

Small sellers absorb the friction. A restructuring that moves inventory ownership from one entity to another triggers fresh GST invoicing, revised e-way bills and reconciliations that most vendors handle with a single accountant. Payment cycles slip by a week or two while the new entity is onboarded. For a seller running on a mid-single-digit net margin and a thin working capital line, a fortnight of delayed settlement is a real problem.

There is also a quieter cost in category planning. Sellers who built inventory for a festive window on the assumption that they would be part of a platform's curated selection find that selection reshuffled while the rules are being reinterpreted. Apparel and small appliances, where seasonal buying commitments are made months ahead, are the most exposed.

"We were told in July that our listings would carry the same badge through Diwali, and by September we were on a different seller account shipping from a different fulfilment centre," said the proprietor of a home furnishing brand that sells from Jaipur.
What real enforcement would need

Officials privately concede that the current toolkit is mismatched to the problem. Establishing an inventory-model breach requires showing ownership or control over goods, and control is demonstrated through contracts that platforms are not obliged to file with anyone. A meaningful enforcement regime would need disclosure: periodic reporting of seller concentration by category, related-party transaction summaries, and the terms of fulfilment and advertising arrangements.

That is a heavier compliance burden than the sector has faced, and it cuts against the government's other objective of keeping platforms investing in warehousing, logistics and small-town seller onboarding. The national e-commerce policy has sat in draft for years partly because these objectives pull in different directions.

In the meantime the cycle repeats. A complaint is filed, a review begins, structures are adjusted, volumes wobble, and the market settles into a shape close to where it started. The sellers who can afford compliance advice adapt. The ones who cannot simply wait for the next reshuffle.

title: The dark store maths that will decide quick commerce's next 200 cities
dek: Ten-minute delivery works where density is high and riders are plentiful. Beyond the metros, both assumptions get considerably harder to hold.

body.text: A quick commerce dark store is a small and unglamorous unit: two to four thousand square feet, no customers, shelves arranged by picking frequency rather than by category, and a cold room in one corner. What it does is convert a delivery promise into a fixed cost. Everything that follows in the business model is a fight over how many orders can be pushed through that fixed cost each day.

In dense metro catchments, the fight is close to won. Stores in parts of Bengaluru, Mumbai and Gurugram routinely run well over a thousand orders a day, and at that volume the rent, the store manager, the pickers and the electricity spread thin enough that contribution per order turns positive. The question the sector is now arguing about is what happens when the same box is dropped into Nashik, Raipur or Madurai.
The answer, on current evidence, is that almost every variable moves the wrong way at once.
Density is the whole model

Ten-minute delivery is a geometry problem before it is a technology problem. A store serves a radius of roughly two to three kilometres, and within that circle it needs enough households ordering often enough to keep riders in near-continuous motion. Metro catchments deliver that through vertical density: a single high-rise cluster can generate more orders than several square kilometres of low-rise housing.

Tier-2 cities are horizontally spread. The same population is distributed across a wider area, which pushes average delivery distance up and rider trips per hour down. Operators compensate by widening the radius, which stretches the promise from ten minutes to fifteen or twenty, which in turn softens the behavioural trigger that made the category work in the first place.

Order values do rise in smaller cities, partly because customers consolidate rather than treating the app as a top-up. That helps, but not enough on its own. A larger basket spreads delivery cost over more rupees only if the delivery cost itself has not risen faster, and in a spread-out city it usually has.
The labour question nobody wants on the record

Rider economics is where the model is most exposed. The metro version relies on a large, flexible pool of workers willing to take short trips at low per-order rates, topped up with peak-hour incentives. That pool exists in Delhi and Bengaluru because migration keeps refilling it. In a tier-2 city the same pool is smaller, better informed about local alternatives, and less willing to work a split shift for the same payout.

Operators respond with higher guarantees, which raises cost per order at precisely the point in a new market where volumes are thin. Some are experimenting with fixed-shift employment for a core group and gig arrangements at the margin, which improves reliability but reintroduces the fixed cost the gig model was designed to avoid.

"In a metro I can staff a Saturday evening peak straight from the app, in a smaller city I have to call people the previous night and promise them a number," said an operations lead who runs about forty stores across two states.

Social security adds another layer of uncertainty. The labour codes contemplate aggregator contributions to a welfare fund for platform workers, and several states have moved on their own gig worker legislation, with Rajasthan and Karnataka among the first. Whatever the final shape, the sector is planning for a cost line that does not currently sit in most unit economics decks.
Assortment is not portable

The metro assortment leans on packaged convenience: ready meals, imported snacks, chilled beverages, personal care. A large share of that catalogue simply does not sell outside the top cities, where the same shelf space is better used for staples, fresh produce and regional brands that the national buying team has never listed.

That forces a genuinely different operating discipline. Fresh produce carries wastage, staples carry low margins and high weight, and regional brands have to be sourced through distributors who are not integrated into anyone's supply chain software. A store carrying the metro assortment in a smaller city will show poor availability on the items customers actually want, and availability, not speed, is what drives repeat ordering.
A narrow but real route to profitability

None of this makes the expansion irrational. The costs that do fall in smaller cities are meaningful: commercial rent for a three thousand square foot unit can be a third of the metro rate, and store staffing is cheaper. If an operator can take a store to a few hundred orders a day with a locally tuned assortment and a fifteen-minute promise, the contribution maths works, just on a slower ramp than investors have been trained to expect.

The operators being most disciplined about this are opening in clusters rather than planting single stores, so a city gets three or four dark stores at once and shares a common local supply line. They are also accepting a longer path to store-level breakeven, in the range of several quarters rather than a few months.
"The mistake is treating a tier-2 city as a metro with cheaper rent," said a category head at a Bengaluru quick commerce firm, "because the customer, the catalogue and the rider are all different."

For kirana stores in these cities, the arrival of a dark store is less an extinction event than a margin squeeze on the fastest-moving two hundred items. Distributors already report that their own route-to-market economics change when a single dark store absorbs a chunk of a locality's impulse purchases. That reordering of the distribution chain, rather than the ten-minute promise itself, is what will shape Indian retail over the next few years.

title: Inside the audit table where online apparel returns are judged
dek: Reverse logistics has become a forensic operation, and the cost of a disputed verdict falls hardest on small sellers with no leverage.

body.text: The parcel arrives back at a returns processing centre off the Delhi-Jaipur highway about six days after it left. It is opened at a bench under a fixed overhead camera, and a young auditor works through a checklist on a handheld terminal: brand tag present, security tag intact, no odour, no makeup marks on the collar, weight within tolerance of the outbound record.

Within ninety seconds the garment is graded. Grade A goes back into sellable inventory. Grade B goes to a liquidation lot. Grade C becomes a claim. Those ninety seconds decide whether a seller in Tiruppur gets paid for the shirt, and whether a customer in Lucknow gets a refund.

Reverse logistics used to be a cost centre nobody examined closely. In fashion, where a substantial share of orders come back, it has become one of the most heavily instrumented parts of Indian e-commerce, and one of the most contested.
How a returns problem became a fraud problem

The bulk of apparel returns are ordinary: wrong size, colour different from the photograph, buyer's remorse. Platforms accept this as the price of selling clothes without a trial room, and the entire category is priced with an assumed return rate built in.

A smaller share is not ordinary. Auditors describe three recurring patterns. The first is wardrobing, where the item is worn once for an occasion and returned inside the window, usually detectable through faint wear at the underarms or a missing security tag. The second is substitution, where a cheaper garment of similar weight is returned in place of the one ordered, which is why outbound weight is now recorded at packing. The third is the empty or short parcel, sometimes with a bag of comparable mass inside.
None of these are new. What is new is that platforms now hold enough data to identify accounts that do it repeatedly, and enough legal caution to be careful about what they do next.

"We can see the pattern on an account within three or four orders," said a fraud analytics manager at a logistics firm that handles returns for several fashion brands, "but proving it to a standard we would put in a letter is a different exercise."
The evidence problem

The audit bench exists to produce evidence. Cameras record the opening of every high-value parcel, packing stations capture outbound weight and a photograph of the sealed bag, and the courier scans the pickup at the customer's door. In theory the chain is complete.

In practice it breaks in predictable places. Doorstep quality checks, where the delivery partner is expected to inspect the returned item before accepting it, are done in a hurry and under pressure from the customer. Weight tolerances are set loose enough to avoid rejecting legitimate returns, which leaves room for substitution with a similar garment. And a parcel that passes through three facilities has three points at which a shortage could have occurred, which is precisely the ambiguity that makes claims hard to settle.

Platforms have responded by tightening the customer-facing side: shorter return windows on some categories, tags that must remain attached, exchange offered ahead of refund, and account-level restrictions for buyers with abnormal return rates. Consumer forums have pushed back on the more aggressive versions of this, and the sector is conscious that a wrongly blocked customer is a reputational cost as well as a lost one.
Who actually pays

When a return is graded as a claim, someone absorbs the loss. On marketplace terms the seller usually does, unless they can produce outbound packing evidence, which requires them to have captured it at their own facility in the first place. Larger brands run packing lines with cameras and weight capture as a matter of course. A small vendor packing two hundred orders a day in a rented unit in Tiruppur or Ludhiana often does not.

The result is an evidentiary asymmetry that maps neatly onto seller size. Vendors describe claim recovery rates that vary widely depending on whether they sit inside a platform's managed fulfilment programme or ship themselves. The dispute process is functional but slow, and for a garment worth a few hundred rupees most small sellers write it off rather than spend a week on it.
"For anything under about a thousand rupees we do not contest it any more, because the paperwork costs more than the shirt," said a Tiruppur manufacturer who sells knitwear on three platforms.
The economics of the second life

Everything that does not go back into sellable inventory enters a secondary market that has grown its own infrastructure. Grade B lots are sold by weight or by carton to liquidators who resell through offline wholesale channels, discount racks in smaller towns and, increasingly, their own online storefronts. Prices are a fraction of the original, and the buyer is usually taking the lot unseen.

This second life matters more than its size suggests, because it sets the floor on what a returned item is worth and therefore how much a platform is willing to spend inspecting one. If a garment recovers a meaningful share of its value through liquidation, an elaborate audit is not worth the labour. If it recovers almost nothing, the incentive shifts towards catching abuse earlier, at the doorstep.

That calculation explains why the most consequential change of the last two years has happened at the customer's door rather than inside the warehouse. Doorstep verification, done properly, removes the ambiguity that makes claims unwinnable. Done badly, it turns delivery partners into arbitrators of disputes they have thirty seconds and no training to resolve.

title: Packaging plants get the nod while the fab question stays open
dek: A widening set of assembly and test approvals is building a real ecosystem, but India's front-end ambitions still hinge on customers rather than capital.

body.text: The India Semiconductor Mission has spent the last two years approving a category of project that attracts less attention than a fabrication plant and is considerably easier to build: assembly, testing, marking and packaging units, known in the industry as ATMP or OSAT.

Sanand in Gujarat has two. Assam's Jagiroad has one under construction on a scale large enough to change a district's labour market. Sites in Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha are at various stages of approval or evaluation. The fiscal support formula, a share of project cost from the Centre matched by additional state incentives, has proved durable enough that state industry departments now compete on land, power tariffs and effluent infrastructure rather than on the headline subsidy.
What has not yet been settled is the harder half of the plan.
Why back-end first was the right sequence

Packaging is capital-hungry but not capital-absurd. An assembly and test line costs a fraction of a leading-edge fab, uses process equipment available without the export-control complications attached to advanced lithography, and can be staffed with engineers and technicians drawn from existing electronics manufacturing.

It also earns revenue sooner. A packaging plant can qualify with a customer and begin shipping within a couple of years of ground-breaking, whereas a fab's ramp is measured in yield learning curves that take longer and cost more to climb. For a programme that has to demonstrate results to a finance ministry, that difference matters.

The strategic argument is separate and stronger. Advanced packaging is where a growing share of performance improvement now comes from, as chiplet architectures and higher-density interconnect substitute for transistor scaling. A country that establishes credible packaging capability is not doing the low-value part of the chain.

"Ten years ago packaging was where you sent the wafer to be put in plastic," said a senior engineer at an OSAT under construction in western India, "and now it is where a large part of the design problem gets solved."
The supplier ecosystem is the real test

A packaging plant needs substrates, lead frames, bonding wire, moulding compound, high-purity chemicals and specialty gases, and it needs all of them qualified. Qualification is slow: a customer will not accept a change of material supplier without a requalification cycle that can run several months.

Almost all of this is imported today. Organic substrates in particular are a concentrated global business, and substrate lead times have been a constraint for the industry worldwide. Domestic production of substrates and lead frames is the single most useful thing India could add to the chain over the next few years, and it is being pursued through electronics component manufacturing incentives rather than through the semiconductor mission itself.

Utilities are less discussed and equally binding. Packaging is not as thirsty as a front-end fab, but it still needs ultrapure water, uninterrupted power at tight quality tolerances and treated effluent capacity. Gujarat's advantage at Sanand and Dholera is largely that this infrastructure was planned alongside the plots rather than retrofitted after allotment.
The design-to-fab gap

India has design talent at scale. A very large share of the world's chip design engineering hours are worked here, across captive centres and independent services firms in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Noida. Almost none of that design work is manufactured in India.

Closing that gap requires a fab with a process node and a customer list. The approved front-end projects target mature nodes aimed at automotive, industrial and power applications, which is the right commercial choice: mature-node demand is durable, qualification is achievable, and the competition is on cost and reliability rather than on the frontier.

The risk sits on the demand side. A mature-node fab needs anchor customers willing to commit volume years in advance, and Indian automotive and industrial buyers have historically bought finished modules rather than chips. Building that domestic pull, through automotive electronics localisation and power electronics for electric vehicles, is a slower policy project than approving a plant, and it depends on decisions taken in vehicle programmes rather than in MeitY.
What to watch next

Three indicators will say more than any approval announcement. The first is whether an Indian packaging line completes customer qualification and ships in volume, which is the moment the ecosystem becomes real to global buyers. The second is whether component suppliers, particularly substrate and specialty chemical firms, commit to Indian plants without a dedicated subsidy of their own.

The third is people. The mission's training targets run into the tens of thousands of engineers, and the institutions doing the work, including the design linked incentive scheme and university tie-ups, are producing designers faster than process and equipment engineers. A fab needs the second kind in quantity, and that pipeline barely exists today.

"We can hire a hundred verification engineers in a month, and it takes us a year to find one person who has actually run a diffusion furnace," said a hiring manager at a semiconductor firm setting up in Gujarat.

The programme's own officials are candid that the sequencing was deliberate and that the fab timelines carry more execution risk than the packaging ones. On the current trajectory, India will be a packaging country with a design industry for several years before it is a manufacturing one, which is a more modest claim than the announcements suggest and a more defensible one.

title: Before the first wafer: the gases, water and vendors a fab needs on site
dek: India's chip plants will turn on unglamorous inputs: nitrogen at the fence line, water purified to parts per trillion, and service engineers within an hour.

body.text: A semiconductor fab is usually described as a cleanroom full of expensive machines. Operationally it is closer to a chemical plant with a very demanding customer inside it.

Bulk nitrogen, hydrogen, argon and helium. Specialty gases delivered in cylinders with parts-per-billion purity guarantees. Ultrapure water produced on site from a municipal supply through a multi-stage plant that strips out ions, organics, dissolved oxygen and particles down to thresholds no other industry cares about. Chemicals delivered daily. Effluent treated before it leaves. All of it available without interruption, because an unplanned stop mid-process scraps wafers.
This is the part of the India semiconductor programme that has been building quietly at Sanand and Dholera while public attention went to approvals and equity structures.
Nitrogen at the fence line

The largest single utility requirement is nitrogen, used to purge tools and blanket processes, and consumed in volumes that make trucking it impractical. The standard arrangement globally is an air separation unit built at the plant boundary by an industrial gas company under a long-term take-or-pay contract, feeding the fab directly through a pipeline measured in metres rather than kilometres.

India has capable industrial gas players and a long history of on-site air separation for steel and refining. The semiconductor requirement differs mainly in purity and in tolerance for interruption. A steel plant can ride through a brief supply dip. A fab counts the cost in scrapped wafer starts and a contaminated tool that has to be requalified.

Specialty gases are a harder problem. Electronic-grade silane, ammonia, tungsten hexafluoride, chlorine-based etchants and the fluorinated gases used in deposition come from a small number of global firms, and a share of the world's electronic-grade neon and related rare gases has been subject to supply disruption in recent years for geopolitical reasons. Fabs manage this with multi-sourcing and inventory, both of which cost working capital.
Water, measured differently

Ultrapure water is not filtered drinking water. It is water stripped of essentially everything, then kept moving in a recirculating loop so that it does not pick anything up again. A fab of meaningful scale needs millions of litres a day of incoming raw water to produce it, and recycles a large fraction internally to keep the net draw manageable.

Siting decisions in Gujarat reflect this. Dholera's plan pairs the industrial zone with a dedicated water conveyance from the Narmada system, and the state's pitch to investors has leaned on assured allocation rather than on tariff. That is the correct emphasis: a fab will pay for water, but it cannot plan around uncertainty in supply.

The other half is discharge. Fab effluent carries fluoride, acids and solvents, and requires treatment before release along with monitoring that state pollution control boards will scrutinise closely. Building this capacity at industrial-park level rather than plant level is cheaper and easier to regulate, and it is one of the genuine advantages of a planned node over a greenfield site chosen for land price.
"The water question is never how much, it is whether the allocation holds in a bad monsoon year," said a utilities consultant who has worked on two proposed fab sites in western India.
Vendors within an hour

Process equipment arrives from a handful of global manufacturers, and the equipment is only half the transaction. Each tool needs field service engineers, spares held locally, and calibration support. Tool downtime is measured in hours of lost production, so equipment makers position service depots close to fab clusters and staff them ahead of demand.

This is the clustering logic that made Hsinchu and Dresden work, and it is why the location of India's second and third plants matters more than the first. A single isolated fab has to fund its own vendor presence. Three plants within a couple of hours of each other can support a shared service ecosystem, a local spares warehouse and a training pipeline that vendors are willing to invest in.

Below the tool vendors sits a longer tail of suppliers that rarely makes headlines: cleanroom construction and certification, chemical delivery systems, high-purity piping and orbital welding, vibration isolation, gas cabinet fabrication, and the specialist contractors who install and validate all of it. Much of this capability already exists in India through pharmaceutical plant construction, which enforces similar cleanliness disciplines, and several of those firms are now retooling for electronics.
The realistic sequence

None of this can be built after a fab is commissioned. Utilities and vendor presence lead the plant by a year or more, which is why the current phase, unglamorous and largely invisible, is the one that determines whether announced timelines hold.

The measurable signals are specific. Watch for on-site air separation units under construction at approved sites, for specialty gas firms announcing Indian cylinder filling and analysis facilities, for equipment makers opening service centres in Ahmedabad or Bengaluru, and for the first Indian companies qualifying as suppliers of high-purity chemicals to a semiconductor customer. Each of those is a smaller announcement than a fab approval and a considerably better indicator of progress.
"You can import a tool, you cannot import a technician who can be on site in ninety minutes at two in the morning," said a project manager involved in commissioning a packaging plant in Gujarat.

title: In Jagiroad, a chip plant arrives ahead of the workforce it needs
dek: Assam's packaging unit is rewiring a small town's labour market, and the training pipeline is being built at the same time as the cleanroom.

body.text: The road from Guwahati to Jagiroad runs past paddy, a paper mill that closed years ago and left the town wary of large industrial promises, and then a stretch of construction traffic that was not there two years ago.

Jagiroad, in Morigaon district, is the site of an assembly and test plant that will package semiconductors for automotive, communications and consumer applications. It is the first project of its kind in the Northeast, and the local economy has begun rearranging itself around the construction phase long before the first chip ships.

Rents in the town have risen. Guesthouses that used to serve occasional government travellers are booked out by contractors. A stretch of shops near the main junction has turned over to construction supplies and tiffin services. Whether any of this survives the transition from building the plant to operating it is the question people here actually ask.
What the plant needs from the town

A packaging line is less engineer-heavy than a front-end fab and more technician-heavy. The bulk of the workforce operates and maintains die attach, wire bonding, moulding, plating and test equipment, works in a cleanroom environment on rotating shifts, and follows procedures where deviation is not tolerated.

That profile is trainable. It requires a diploma-level technical education, literacy sufficient for standard operating procedures, and the discipline of gowning and process compliance, which is closer to a pharmaceutical plant than to general engineering. It does not require a masters degree in microelectronics.

It does require volume. A plant of this scale employs a few thousand people directly at full ramp and several times that indirectly, through logistics, canteen services, maintenance contracting and housing. Assam's polytechnics and industrial training institutes produce diploma holders in adequate numbers. What they have not historically produced is people trained for cleanroom discipline, because there was no cleanroom in the state to train for.
Building the pipeline in parallel

The response has been a set of tie-ups between the company, the state skill development authority and technical institutions in Assam, along with placements at existing facilities elsewhere in the country and abroad. A first cohort of local recruits has been sent out of state for training on live lines, which is the only way to learn equipment behaviour that a classroom cannot simulate.

Faculty is the constraint that gets the least attention. Teaching cleanroom practice requires instructors who have worked in one. The state is importing that expertise on contract, and the longer-term plan depends on early cohorts returning as trainers, a cycle that takes years to close.

"The first batch is the expensive batch," said a training coordinator working with a technical institute in Guwahati, "because everything after that can be taught by people who have already done the job here."

Retention is the second worry, and a specific one for the Northeast. Young technicians who acquire a scarce and portable skill become attractive to plants in Gujarat and Karnataka that can pay more. The counterargument, which local recruiters make openly, is that a job at home at a decent wage beats a marginally better job two thousand kilometres away, and that this plant is the first time that trade-off has existed here at all.
The town's memory of industry

Scepticism in Jagiroad is not abstract. The paper mill that shut left unpaid dues and a long dispute behind it, and older residents raise it whenever the new plant comes up. The lesson they draw is not that industry fails but that a single-employer town is fragile, and that the value of the project depends on whether anything grows around it.

There are early signs of that. Packaging materials, industrial gases, logistics and calibration services all have to come from somewhere, and some of it will come from Guwahati rather than from outside the state. Whether substrate handling, tooling or precision component work follows depends on volumes that do not yet exist.

Infrastructure is being upgraded in the meantime: power evacuation, road widening, and a water supply engineered to a standard the district has not previously needed. The plant's requirement for uninterrupted quality power is being met through dedicated feeders, an investment that incidentally benefits the surrounding area.
The measure of success

The straightforward test is whether the plant qualifies with customers and ramps to designed capacity. Packaging is a business of qualification cycles: a customer audits the line, runs sample lots, tests reliability over months and only then commits volume. That process is well under way at plants elsewhere in India and has not begun here.

The local test is different and slower. It is whether a nineteen-year-old from Morigaon who joins as a trainee operator is, in ten years, running a shift here, or has left for Sanand. On that question everyone in Jagiroad is guessing, including the people doing the hiring.
"My son finished his diploma in Nagaon and was going to Bengaluru," said a shopkeeper on the road to the plant, "and now he is waiting to see what happens here first."

title: Services exporters caught in the intermediary tag as refunds age
dek: Back-office and captive units say a single word in a contract decides whether their billing is a zero-rated export or a taxable intermediary supply.

body.text: The paperwork has a rhythm to it by now. Once a quarter, the finance team at a mid-sized business support firm in Pune assembles the same bundle: master services agreement, statements of work, invoices, foreign inward remittance certificates, and a covering note explaining why the company believes it sells services to an overseas client on its own account. Once a quarter the refund claim goes in. Then it waits.

The question the file turns on is whether the firm is an exporter of services or an intermediary. Exports are zero rated, and accumulated input tax credit comes back as cash. Intermediary services are treated as supplied at the location of the supplier, which means India, which means tax at the standard rate and no refund. Same work, same client, same dollars arriving in the bank. Different noun in a contract, very different cash position.

That distinction now runs through a broad slice of the services economy: procurement desks, vendor management offices, marketing support units, engineering support centres, claims processing teams, and the growing population of captive units that bill a foreign parent on a cost-plus basis. Tax advisers say contested refund claims have thickened as more of this work shifted to Indian entities invoicing related parties abroad.
Where the line gets drawn

The statutory test is narrow on paper. An intermediary arranges or facilitates a supply of goods or services between two other persons and does not supply the main service on its own account. A firm that performs the service itself, and bills for it, is not an intermediary. Departmental circulars have said as much, and have added that the mere use of the word support in a contract does not settle the matter.

In practice the reading happens clause by clause. Officers look for words like liaison, coordination, on behalf of, and on account of. They look at whether the Indian entity signs anything with the end customer, whether it holds pricing discretion, and whether its fee is a markup on cost or a commission tied to transactions concluded elsewhere. Two firms doing near-identical work can end up on opposite sides of the line because one drafted its agreement in 2016 and the other in 2023.

The result is a body of rulings that does not point in one direction. Advance ruling authorities in different states have reached different conclusions on similar facts, high courts have examined the place of supply rule for intermediaries with mixed outcomes, and appellate benches have sent matters back for fresh reading of contracts. For a company, that means the answer depends partly on where it happens to be registered.
What it costs to be on the wrong side

Firms describe the exposure in working capital terms rather than tax terms. A services exporter with a large domestic cost base accumulates credit on rent, professional fees, software licences and facility management, and expects it back. When claims stall, the amount locked up can reach a low-single-digit share of annual revenue, which is enough to change hiring plans at a company running an operating margin in the low teens.

There is a second cost that shows up on no statement. Deals get repriced. When a foreign parent is told that its Indian delivery unit may attract an eighteen per cent charge it cannot recover, the internal case for adding scope in India weakens against the case for Manila, Krakow or Kuala Lumpur. Several advisers said they had been asked to opine on exactly that comparison during site selection reviews.

"We are not arguing about the tax rate, we are arguing about a noun," said a partner at a tax advisory firm that represents services exporters in Pune and Bengaluru. "The rate has been settled for years. The classification is where the money actually sits."
Contracts rewritten, not always convincingly

The standard remedy is a redraft. Agency language comes out, principal-to-principal language goes in, deliverables are defined as outputs rather than assistance, and the fee is restated as consideration for a defined service. A few firms have gone further and restructured so the Indian entity contracts directly with the end customer, subcontracting nothing back to the parent.

Advisers warn that cosmetic edits do not survive scrutiny, and that they can collide with a company's own transfer pricing file. A captive that tells the income tax department it is a low-risk, routine service provider bearing no market risk is not helped when it tells the indirect tax authority that it is a full principal supplying on its own account. Keeping the two positions consistent has become a compliance exercise of its own.
The zone and GIFT City carve-outs

Units in special economic zones, and in the international financial services centre at GIFT City, sit in a slightly different position, since supplies to a zone unit for authorised operations are themselves zero rated and much of the input chain can be routed without an upfront cash outgo. Firms with a genuine choice have noticed. Some new delivery units have been set up inside zones for reasons that have little to do with the zone's original purpose.

That route is not open to everyone. Existing centres in ordinary commercial buildings in Gurugram, Hyderabad or Chennai cannot relocate to suit a tax reading, and zone units carry their own reporting obligations, net foreign exchange requirements and restrictions on serving the domestic market.

"Every renewal now has a tax clause negotiation attached to it, which was never true five years ago," said a finance controller at a Chennai back-office services company. "Our client is asking us to indemnify a liability that depends on how one officer reads one sentence."
What the industry is asking for

Industry bodies, NASSCOM among them, have pressed for three things: a clarificatory circular listing fact patterns that are not intermediary services, a safe harbour for cost-plus captives that meet defined conditions, and provisional refunds released against a bond while classification is litigated. The last would fix the cash problem without settling the legal one, which is why it is the most likely to move.

None of that is imminent. In the meantime the practical advice being given is unglamorous. Write contracts that describe what the entity actually does rather than what sounded elegant in a template. Keep the transfer pricing study and the indirect tax position aligned. File refunds early enough that a two-year dispute does not quietly become a three-year one.

title: Billing by outcome, not by seat, is rewriting services contracts
dek: Clients are pushing Indian IT and BPM vendors onto per-transaction pricing, and the change is reshaping rosters, reporting and revenue recognition.

body.text: Procurement teams have changed their opening question. Where a renewal conversation once began with rate cards and pyramid ratios, several Indian IT services and business process management vendors say clients now open by asking what they will be charged for a resolved ticket, a processed invoice, a settled claim or an onboarded merchant. The unit of billing is moving away from the seat and the person-month.

The shift is not new in principle. Managed services contracts have carried output pricing for years. What has changed is how far it now reaches into portfolios that were billed by effort until recently, including application maintenance, finance and accounting operations, customer support and parts of infrastructure management.

Behind it sits an uncomfortable arithmetic for vendors. If automation removes effort from a process, effort-based billing passes the saving to the client only when the vendor volunteers it. Clients have stopped waiting to be told. Contracts increasingly carry productivity commitments of several per cent a year and price the work per transaction, leaving the vendor whatever it can squeeze out below that.
Baselining is the real negotiation

Before a per-unit price can be quoted, both sides have to agree what a unit is. Vendors describe months of volume studies before signature: what counts as a ticket, whether a reopened ticket is a new one, how a complex claim is separated from a simple one, what happens during a seasonal peak, and who absorbs volume that falls below a floor.

Those definitions become the dispute surface later. A retail client whose store count grows changes the denominator. A bank that launches a product generates a category of query nobody priced. Most contracts now carry a band, often around a fifth either side of forecast volume, outside which pricing reopens automatically.

Legal teams have adapted by attaching data annexures that run longer than the commercial terms themselves. One vendor said its standard schedule for a mid-sized finance operations deal now includes a full year of monthly volume history, a definitions glossary and an agreed method for reconciling the client's system of record against the vendor's own workflow tool.

"The commercial risk moved to us, so the estimation work moved to us as well," said a delivery head at a business process management firm with centres in Noida and Hyderabad. "We now spend longer pricing a deal than we used to spend staffing one."
What it does to the delivery floor

Inside the centres the change shows up as scheduling rather than headline layoffs. Rosters get built around forecast volume curves instead of fixed shifts. Buffer capacity, once billed to the client, now sits on the vendor's own cost line, which pushes managers towards cross-skilling so that an agent trained on three queues can be moved during a peak.

Utilisation targets rise and the pyramid flattens at the bottom. Work that can be automated is automated first, because the saving accrues to the vendor. What remains is exception handling, which needs more experienced staff, which lifts average cost per person even as the number of people falls.

Managers say the harder change is measurement. Outcome contracts require instrumented workflows tracked at a granularity many older delivery estates were never built for. Several firms have had to rebuild reporting before they could bill at all, and at least one large transition in the sector slipped a quarter for that reason alone.
The finance team inherits the volatility

Revenue recognition gets more complicated. Variable consideration, service credits and penalty clauses have to be estimated and constrained, and revenue is recognised as work is performed rather than as people are billed. Quarterly revenue starts to track client volumes, which are outside the vendor's control.

Unbilled receivables rise in transition quarters, and days sales outstanding can drift while volume reconciliation is argued out. Analysts have begun asking managements to split growth into volume, price and scope, because a flat quarter can now mean a client sold fewer policies rather than a vendor losing share.
Where the model does not fit

Not everything survives the translation. Discretionary transformation work, where scope is genuinely unknown at signature, still prices by effort. Highly regulated processes with unpredictable volumes, such as a remediation programme ordered by a regulator, resist per-unit pricing. So does work whose pace is set by the client's own legacy systems.

Mid-tier vendors face a balance sheet question as well. Outcome pricing usually front-loads investment: transition cost, automation build, tooling, and sometimes a contractual commitment to reduce the unit price over three years. A firm without the cash to fund a loss-making first year simply cannot bid, which is quietly concentrating the larger deals among a handful of buyers.

"We walked away from two deals last year because the year-one economics needed a balance sheet we do not have," said the chief executive of a mid-sized services firm headquartered in Pune. "That is a structural disadvantage, not a sales problem."
The hiring signal

For employment the effect is not a straightforward reduction. Executives point to hiring shifting rather than stopping: fewer entry-level seats attached directly to volume, more demand for process engineers, data analysts, automation developers and contract managers. Campus intake has become lumpier, concentrated in the quarters after large deals close rather than spread evenly through the year.

The wider consequence may fall on the industry's oldest promise. A sector that sold predictable, scalable capacity is being asked to sell measured results instead, and the firms getting there first are rebuilding their sales, pricing and delivery functions in order to do it.

title: In Coimbatore, a capability centre is only as good as its bus roster
dek: A capability centre in Coimbatore runs on bus rosters, diesel gensets and a contract workforce that is only now being brought onto formal payrolls.

body.text: The first shift bus leaves Peelamedu at 5.40 in the morning, on a route the transport contractor redraws every few weeks as staff move house. On a good day it reaches the campus off the Avinashi Road corridor in thirty-eight minutes. On a day when flyover work closes a lane it takes an hour, a floor of analysts starts late, and a reconciliation report reaches a treasury team in Zurich a day behind schedule.
This is what running a global capability centre in a tier-two city actually looks like. Less a real estate decision than a logistics one.

Coimbatore has become one of the more visible test cases, alongside Kochi, Indore, Nagpur, Visakhapatnam, Jaipur and Vadodara. The pull factors are familiar: office rent at a fraction of Bengaluru or Hyderabad, salary differentials in the mid-range roles, lower attrition, and a steady output of engineering and commerce graduates from colleges in and around the district. The friction shows up later, in everything that is not the office itself.
Why the arithmetic works, until it does not

Centre heads describe the cost case as durable at the individual contributor level and fragile at the supervisory level. Analysts, engineers and process associates can be hired locally and retained longer than in the metros, partly because people are near family and are not paying metro rents. Team leads and functional managers with ten to fifteen years in a comparable operation are much harder to find.

The usual fix is a seed team relocated from Bengaluru or Chennai on a two-year assignment, with a housing allowance and a school admission problem attached. Firms that plan for this budget it explicitly. Firms that do not tend to discover, around month nine, that they are flying managers in every week and that the travel line has eaten the rent saving.
The support economy that has to exist first

Almost nothing on the campus is done by the centre's own employees. Security, housekeeping, cafeteria, landscaping, helpdesk, mailroom and transport are all contracted, usually through an integrated facility management provider that in turn subcontracts. A single 1,200-seat floor plate can sit on top of six or seven vendor payrolls, most of them holding people the centre's own HR system never sees.

That layer is where formalisation is happening, slowly and mostly because clients demand it. Multinational parents run vendor audits that ask for provident fund and employee state insurance challans, minimum wage compliance and proof that overtime was paid at statutory rates. Contractors who ran on cash and a register have had to move to biometric attendance and bank transfers to stay on the panel.

The infrastructure side is less negotiable. Centres run dual fibre from separate providers on physically separate last-mile routes, because a single backhoe on Sathy Road has taken out both before. Diesel generators are sized for the whole load, not a partial one. Water arrives partly by tanker in the dry months, and the tanker contract is treated as seriously as the bandwidth contract.

"People think the risk is talent. The risk is the last two kilometres," said a facilities manager who has commissioned three centres in Tamil Nadu. "Road, power, water, fibre. Get those wrong and your service levels are a lottery."
Night shifts and the rules around them

Serving European and North American clients means night and evening shifts, which brings the state's shops and establishments framework into play. Permissions for women to work night shifts come with conditions on written consent, minimum group sizes, transport to the door, and a security escort on the vehicle. Compliance is not merely a document exercise: it changes the route plan, the vehicle count and the cost per seat.

Recruiters say the constraint also shapes who applies. In a city where a substantial share of women graduates live with parents, a documented escort policy and a named transport supervisor are decisive in a way that a salary band is not. Centres that publicise the policy at campus drives report visibly better conversion.
A labour market with other options

Coimbatore is not a company town waiting for an anchor. It has pump manufacturing, textiles, foundries, motors, auto components and a dense small-industry cluster, and its engineering graduates have historically gone into those or left for the metros. The capability centres compete with all of it, and with the quieter option of a family business.

What the centres offer is a formal contract, a payslip, a structured appraisal and, increasingly, a path that does not require moving. What they ask for is English fluency at a level the local schooling system does not uniformly produce, which is why most centres now fund communication training in the first eight weeks and treat it as a cost of doing business rather than a remedial exception.

"Earlier our best students had to leave, and most did not come back," said a placement officer at an engineering college on the Pollachi road. "Now about a fifth of the batch has an option at home. That is new, and it is fragile."
What the city gets, and what it risks

The visible effects are the ordinary ones: apartment rents firming in Saravanampatti and Vilankurichi, cafes that stay open past eleven, a waiting list at two international schools, and a new set of gyms priced for salaried twenty-somethings. Local contractors who once served only manufacturing have added a services vertical.

The risk sits in concentration. A district that builds an office economy on a small number of foreign parents inherits their consolidation decisions. Centre heads privately acknowledge that a portfolio review in a headquarters six thousand kilometres away can undo a decade of local hiring, and that the buffer against it is not incentives but depth: enough separate employers that no single one can hollow the ecosystem out.

title: Authorisation queue lengthens as the private launch pipeline thickens
dek: Launch and satellite operators say approvals, range slots and test facility access have become scheduling constraints as the private pipeline thickens.

body.text: For a sector that measures progress in launches, the binding constraint in Indian space this year is administrative. Private operators preparing launch vehicles, satellite constellations and ground segment build-outs say the interval between filing for authorisation and receiving it has become a planning input in its own right, sitting alongside vehicle readiness and weather windows.

IN-SPACe, the single-window authorisation and regulatory body set up under the Department of Space, now handles a materially wider caseload than it did at inception. Applications span suborbital and orbital launch, satellite operation, earth station and gateway authorisation, and the transfer of technology arrangements that let private firms build on ISRO-developed designs. Each has its own review path.

Nobody in the industry argues for lighter scrutiny. Orbital debris obligations, frequency coordination, national security review and third-party liability all have to be assessed, and a regulator that waves projects through would create problems that outlast any schedule saved. The complaint is narrower: that timelines are not predictable enough to underwrite a launch manifest or an investor milestone.
Three queues, not one

Founders describe three distinct waits that are often confused with each other. The first is the authorisation itself, which turns on technical review, debris mitigation plans, and inter-ministerial consultation. The second is spectrum, which involves the department of telecommunications and international coordination through the ITU, and which runs on its own clock entirely.

The third is facility access. Most Indian launch and satellite firms do not own environmental test capability, static fire stands or clean rooms at the scale they need, and depend on agreements with ISRO centres. Slots at the vibration and thermal vacuum facilities associated with VSSC in Thiruvananthapuram and the Space Applications Centre in Ahmedabad are booked well in advance, and a slipped slot can move a mission by a quarter.

"We plan the vehicle around the test slot, not the other way round," said a mission operations engineer at a Bengaluru launch startup. "If you miss a window at a shared facility you are not waiting a week. You are waiting for the next gap in someone else's campaign."
Range capacity and the second port

At Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, range availability is shared between national missions, commercial flights arranged through NSIL, and private vehicles. Range clearance involves safety corridors, downrange tracking, shipping and aviation notices, and coordination that does not compress easily.

The new launch complex at Kulasekarapattinam in Tamil Nadu's Thoothukudi district is intended to relieve exactly this pressure, and to serve small vehicles flying southward without the dogleg manoeuvre that a launch from Sriharikota needs to avoid overflying Sri Lanka. Operators expect it to matter most for small satellite launch vehicles and dedicated rideshare missions, and least for the heavy national programme, which stays where its infrastructure is.

Until that facility is fully commissioned, the manifest problem persists. Several small launch firms have said publicly that they hold vehicle hardware in various states of integration while range and authorisation timelines settle, which converts fixed cost into idle inventory.
Capital, and the FDI question

Liberalised foreign direct investment norms for space now allow automatic-route investment up to segment-specific ceilings, with higher thresholds for satellite manufacturing, operation and ground segment work than for launch vehicles and associated systems, and full automatic-route treatment for components and subsystems. The intent was to let firms raise growth capital without a case-by-case approval.

Investors say the effect has been real but uneven. Component and subsystem makers report easier conversations with foreign strategic investors. Launch vehicle developers, which sit under the tightest ceiling and the heaviest security review, still find that a foreign lead investor triggers a longer diligence process than a purely domestic round would.

Domestic demand is meanwhile being reshaped by defence and surveillance requirements. Programmes for space-based surveillance and secure communications have created an anchor customer that is not price-driven and not export-dependent, which changes the business case for firms that were previously chasing commercial constellations abroad.
Liability, insurance and a law still pending

India remains a party to the international liability convention, which makes the state liable for damage caused by objects launched from its territory. In the absence of a comprehensive domestic space activities law, the allocation of that liability back to a private operator is handled contractually, through the authorisation conditions and indemnity undertakings rather than through statute.

That works, but it prices badly. Insurers underwriting launch and in-orbit risk for Indian operators say they are pricing legal uncertainty on top of technical uncertainty, and that a statutory framework with defined liability caps would narrow premiums more effectively than any number of successful flights.

"A cap in law is worth more to an underwriter than three clean launches," said a policy adviser who has worked with several Indian space startups on regulatory filings. "Right now every operator is negotiating its own risk allocation from scratch."

Officials have signalled that the framework is being worked on, and that authorisation capacity is being expanded with additional technical reviewers. For companies with hardware built and capital burning, the useful measure will be simpler than any of that: how many weeks the next application takes.

title: The parts problem: India's space startups still wait on qualification
dek: Startups can design a spacecraft faster than they can qualify the parts inside it, and the test queue has become the industry's quiet bottleneck.

body.text: A propellant valve sits in a crate in a Hyderabad workshop, machined, cleaned and documented. It has been there for eleven weeks. Its designer is confident it will work. The problem is that confidence is not a qualification status, and until the part has been through a defined campaign of vibration, thermal cycling, vacuum exposure and leak testing, with records that a customer's reviewer will accept, it cannot fly.

Multiply that crate across dozens of firms and the shape of a bottleneck appears. Indian space startups have got noticeably faster at design, simulation and integration. They have not got faster at proving that a part will survive launch and orbit, because that step depends on test facilities, qualified parts lists and paperwork conventions that were built for a single national programme and are now being asked to serve twenty-odd companies at once.

A review of how a dozen firms handle qualification, based on conversations with procurement leads, test engineers and small manufacturers in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Coimbatore, points to four distinct chokepoints rather than one.
The heritage trap

The first is circular. Buyers of spacecraft want components with flight heritage, meaning parts that have already worked in orbit. A component that has never flown is treated as a risk item, sometimes formally excluded by a customer's parts control board. But a part cannot acquire heritage without flying, and nobody wants to be the mission that gives it the first ride.

The workaround, everywhere, is to buy the first flight. Firms fly new components as passengers on demonstration missions, on rideshare payloads, or on their own technology demonstrators, absorbing the cost purely to generate a flight record. That is affordable for a connector or a sensor. It is much harder for a propulsion component whose demonstration requires most of a spacecraft around it.

Established suppliers abroad enjoy the opposite position: decades of accumulated heritage that an Indian entrant cannot buy at any price. Procurement leads described it as the single most persistent reason an import wins against a domestic part that is cheaper and available sooner.
Test slots are the scarce asset

The second chokepoint is physical. Environmental test capability at the scale space work requires, large shaker tables, thermal vacuum chambers, acoustic cells, EMI and EMC chambers, radiation test beams, exists in India mostly inside ISRO centres and a small number of defence and academic laboratories. Private firms access it through agreements, and access is rationed by national mission schedules.

Several companies said a qualification campaign that needs three to four weeks of chamber time can wait months for the window, and that a failure mid-campaign is punishing twice over: the redesign is quick, the requeue is not. A few have started building modest in-house capability for smaller articles, but a full thermal vacuum facility with cryogenic shrouds is a capital item most seed-stage firms cannot justify.

"The design cycle is now four months and the qualification cycle is fourteen," said a procurement lead at a small satellite manufacturer in Bengaluru. "Every schedule we publish is really a statement about test slot availability, and everyone in the room knows it."
Import lists, lead times and export control

The third is the supply of electrical, electronic and electromechanical parts. Radiation-tolerant processors, space-grade capacitors, certain optocouplers and specialised connectors are largely imported, and the qualified vendor lists that customers accept are dominated by American and European suppliers. Lead times of forty weeks and longer are routine, and allocation during a global shortage does not favour a first-time Indian buyer.

Export control adds a second layer. Parts controlled under United States regulations carry licensing conditions and end-use documentation that complicate resale and re-export, which is one reason many Indian teams now specify parts that are free of those controls even at a performance penalty. India's own SCOMET list governs the outbound direction, and firms exporting subsystems have had to build compliance functions earlier than their headcount would suggest.

Screening offers a partial escape. Buying commercial parts and subjecting them to upscreening, burn-in, lot sample testing and radiation characterisation is cheaper than buying space-grade equivalents, and is standard practice for short-life low earth orbit missions. It also transfers the qualification burden back onto the test queue described above.
The MSME layer nobody planned for

Mechanical parts tell a more encouraging story. Machining, forging, precision fabrication, harness assembly and composite structures are being supplied by small and medium manufacturers in Coimbatore, Pune, Hyderabad and the Bengaluru industrial belt, many of which came from automotive, aerospace or pump manufacturing and already held quality certifications.

The gap for them is not capability but documentation. Space work demands material traceability to the heat lot, controlled processes, non-conformance reporting and a configuration record that survives audit years later. Firms that have made the transition describe eighteen months of paperwork discipline before their first accepted delivery, funded largely out of their own working capital.

"The machine was never the problem. The travellers, the certificates and the audit trail were," said the proprietor of a precision engineering unit near Coimbatore that now supplies structural parts to two launch companies. "We hired a quality engineer before we won a single order."
What would actually shift it

The asks are consistent across the firms interviewed. Independent, commercially operated environmental test laboratories, so that qualification does not compete with national mission schedules. A published Indian qualified parts list with defined acceptance criteria, so a domestic component has a route to recognition. Common facilities for radiation testing. And a standing demonstration flight programme that lets new parts acquire heritage predictably rather than opportunistically.

Some of this is moving. IN-SPACe has funded technical development at several firms and has been opening departmental facilities to private users under formal agreements. Whether that converts into shorter queues depends on capacity being added rather than merely shared, which is a capital question that the sector's current revenue base does not obviously answer.

title: Around the second launch port, Thoothukudi's land market moved first
dek: Long before a rocket lifts from the Thoothukudi coast, land prices, coaching classes and fishing rights are already being renegotiated.

body.text: The road south from Tiruchendur runs past palmyra stands, salt pans and small churches, and until recently it carried mostly fish trucks and cement lorries. It now carries surveyors. Along a stretch of coast near Kulasekarapattinam, in Tamil Nadu's Thoothukudi district, the second Indian launch port is taking shape, and the local economy has begun rearranging itself around a facility that has not yet flown a rocket.

Land is the first market to move, as it always is. Brokers in the nearby towns say enquiries now come from Chennai, Madurai and Bengaluru, and that plots along the approach roads have been transacting at multiples of what they fetched three years ago. Much of the trade is speculative and some of it is in land whose title will not survive close reading.

What the launch port is for is narrower than the excitement suggests. The site is intended primarily for small satellite launch vehicles, which can fly almost due south from this coast into polar and sun-synchronous orbits without the dogleg manoeuvre a Sriharikota launch requires to avoid overflying Sri Lanka. Avoiding that manoeuvre recovers payload capacity, which for a small vehicle is the difference between a viable mission and a marginal one.
Why this particular coast

Site selection for a launch range is unromantic. It needs an unobstructed downrange corridor over water, a sparse population within the safety zone, reasonable road and rail access, a port within reach for oversized hardware, and enough flat land for integration buildings, propellant storage and a safety perimeter that nobody may build inside.

This stretch scores well on most of those. The Bay of Bengal opens south with little shipping density close to shore. Thoothukudi port handles heavy cargo. The rail line and the highway network to Tirunelveli and Madurai are serviceable. The population is coastal and clustered, which makes the safety zone question a matter of specific hamlets rather than a dispersed settlement pattern.

The costs are equally specific. Salt pans and fishing grounds are livelihoods, not empty land. Coastal regulation rules govern what can be built how close to the shore. And a launch range imposes a permanent restriction on what may happen around it, which in a district with an active industrial pipeline is not a trivial encumbrance.
The fishing question

Fishermen from the hamlets along this coast work in mechanised and country boats, and the concern raised repeatedly at district hearings is not the land acquisition but the sea. A launch requires a cleared maritime corridor, notified in advance, within which boats may not operate. On a launch day and the days around it, a section of the fishing ground closes.

For a small vehicle programme flying occasionally, the disruption is manageable. For the flight rate the facility is designed to sustain eventually, it is a recurring loss of fishing days that falls on people whose income does not average well across a month. Panchayat representatives have asked for a notification protocol in Tamil, delivered through the local fisheries cooperative rather than through general notices, and for compensation tied to notified closure days.

"We are not against the rocket. We are asking to be told three days ahead, in writing, and to be paid for the days we cannot go out," said a member of a fishermen's cooperative near the site. "So far we hear about things after they are decided."
Who gets the jobs

The employment arithmetic is where local expectation and industrial reality diverge most sharply. A launch range is not a factory. The permanent technical staff, range safety officers, propulsion technicians, telemetry and tracking engineers, quality inspectors, number in the hundreds rather than the thousands, and most will be recruited nationally or transferred from existing centres.

The larger local opportunity is construction during the build phase, and then the service layer that follows: transport, catering, security, housekeeping, warehousing, equipment maintenance, and the accommodation trade that grows around any facility hosting visiting engineering teams. Those are real jobs. They are not the engineering careers described in the district's coaching class advertisements, which have already begun promising placements at the spaceport.

Polytechnics and industrial training institutes in Tirunelveli and Thoothukudi have started adjusting course mixes towards instrumentation, welding certification, industrial electrical work and non-destructive testing, which is a more honest read of where local hiring will actually occur. Whether the certification quality matches what a range contractor will accept is an open question that will be answered at the first tender.
The long wait

Launch infrastructure takes years, and the intermediate period is where local goodwill is usually spent. Roads get dug up for utilities. Water allocations get argued over in a district that is not water-rich. Property expectations rise faster than the payroll does, which prices young families out of towns their parents could afford.

District officials say the mitigation is sequencing: land compensation settled early and visibly, a fisheries protocol agreed before the first launch rather than after it, and skills programmes matched to tenders that actually exist. The alternative, visible at other large projects along this coastline, is a decade of litigation running parallel to the construction schedule.

"The technical schedule is the easy part of this project," said a former range engineer who now advises on launch site planning. "The hard part is that a spaceport needs a neighbourhood that still wants it in year eight."

For now the coast is quiet in the way it always was, minus the surveyors and the occasional convoy of equipment heading south. The palmyra crop is being harvested. The salt pans are working. Somewhere in the middle distance a boundary wall is going up around a piece of land that will, eventually, be the reason anyone outside the district knows the name of this place.

title: Reverse flips gather pace as startups redomicile ahead of Indian listings
dek: A widening set of India-facing companies is unwinding overseas holding structures, drawn home by domestic listing valuations and a shorter path to market.

body.text: Moving a holding company from Singapore or Delaware back to India was, until recently, treated as a last resort. Founders did it when the overseas structure had outlived its purpose and the cost of unwinding was finally smaller than the cost of maintaining it. That calculation has shifted. Over the past two years a steady stream of consumer internet, fintech and software companies has begun redomiciling to India, and the lawyers and tax advisers who handle these transactions say their pipelines now stretch well into the next financial year.

The trigger is not sentiment, whatever the conference panels suggest. It is the listing window. Domestic exchanges have absorbed a run of technology issues at valuations that boards did not expect to see onshore even three years ago, and the price discovery gap that once justified a Cayman or Mauritius parent has narrowed. For a company that intends to list in India within three years, an offshore holding structure has become an obstacle to be dismantled rather than an asset to be defended.

Dismantling it is rarely quick. Bringing a parent home means either a cross-border merger approved by the National Company Law Tribunal or an outbound share swap that crystallises capital gains in the jurisdiction being left behind. Both routes involve regulators in two countries who have no particular reason to coordinate their timelines.
The mechanics of coming home

The merger route has become the more common of the two. A company incorporated overseas merges into its Indian subsidiary, shareholders of the foreign entity receive shares in the Indian company, and the foreign shell is struck off. On paper it is clean. In practice the sequencing is unforgiving: the scheme has to clear the tribunal, the central bank rules on cross-border amalgamations have to be satisfied, and the foreign regulator has to accept that the entity it supervises is disappearing into another jurisdiction. Advisers describe timelines of twelve to eighteen months as normal, and longer where the cap table includes sovereign or pension money.

The second route, a share swap, is faster but expensive. Shareholders exchange their holdings in the foreign parent for shares in an Indian entity, and the exchange is a taxable event in most jurisdictions. For early investors sitting on paper gains accumulated across several rounds, the bill can be large enough to stall the whole exercise. Companies that have gone this way tend to have concentrated cap tables and a small number of institutional holders who can be brought to a common position in a few meetings rather than a few quarters.

There is a third complication that shows up late. Employee stock options issued by an offshore parent do not simply migrate. They have to be cancelled and reissued under an Indian scheme, with fresh valuations, fresh perquisite tax treatment at exercise, and in some cases fresh vesting clocks that employees never agreed to. Several companies have discovered that the option conversion, not the merger, is the part that generates internal friction.
"The merger is a legal problem with known steps," said a partner at a Bengaluru law firm that has run four redomiciling schemes. "The option pool is a human problem, and nobody budgets time for it."
The tax bill nobody quotes upfront

Public discussion of reverse flipping tends to focus on the headline question of whether the transaction attracts tax at all. The more useful question is where the value sits. If the intellectual property, the customer contracts and the revenue have always been recognised in the Indian operating company, the foreign parent is close to an empty box and the transfer prices are defensible. If the offshore entity has been booking licensing income or holding the brand, the exercise turns into a valuation argument with the tax authority about what is actually being moved.

Advisers say the companies that complete the process smoothly are those that spent the previous two or three years quietly reversing intra-group arrangements, shifting intellectual property ownership onshore in stages and letting the offshore parent thin out. The ones that run into trouble attempt it in a single step, weeks after deciding to file for an initial public offering, and find that diligence for the offer document surfaces every unresolved position at once.
Investors recalculate the exit

For funds, the shift changes the arithmetic of an exit. An offshore holding company allowed a foreign limited partner to receive proceeds in dollars without confronting Indian withholding or the mechanics of repatriation. An Indian listing means selling on the domestic exchanges, dealing with lock-in requirements applicable to pre-issue shareholders, and accepting rupee proceeds. Several global funds have restructured their India feeder vehicles in response, and some have simply accepted the friction because the alternative, waiting for an overseas listing that may never come, is worse.

Domestic institutional investors read it differently. Mutual funds and insurers that were structurally unable to buy an offshore-parented company at the growth stage can now participate in pre-IPO rounds of the same business. That has widened the pool of late-stage capital available onshore at a time when global crossover funds have been selective, and it has given companies a reason to complete the redomiciling before, rather than after, their final private round.
"We are being asked about the domicile in the first meeting now, not the fourth," said an investment banker who works on pre-IPO placements in Mumbai.
A pipeline that depends on the window staying open

The obvious risk is that the entire logic rests on domestic listing conditions holding. Redomiciling is a one-way, expensive and slow decision taken on the assumption that the public market will still be receptive when the process ends a year or more later. Companies that began the exercise in a strong market and arrive at the filing stage in a weak one will have paid the cost without collecting the benefit, and will find it far harder to go back offshore than it was to come home.

Policy has, so far, moved in the same direction as the trend.
