Both descriptions are accurate, and the tension between them surfaces every season when app-based operators attempt to work the route from the railhead.

The compromise most towns have reached is territorial. Aggregators bring visitors up from the plains, local taxis handle movement within the hills, and the boundary is enforced socially rather than legally. It holds because neither side benefits from a confrontation during the season, and it is renegotiated, informally, most years.
Water, waste and the carrying capacity argument

The town's water supply is a gravity scheme drawing from springs above the settlement, augmented by pumping in the dry months. Its design population is a fraction of what occupies the town on a long weekend in June, and hotels bridge the gap with tankers drawn from sources further down the valley.

Solid waste is the more visible problem. Collection is sized for resident households, and the peak season generates a volume of packaging and bottles that overwhelms both the vehicles and the disposal site, which sits on a slope above a stream in the way that most hill town sites do. Segregation at source is mandated and inconsistently practised, and the material that has value leaves with private aggregators while the rest accumulates.

This is the factual basis for the carrying capacity petitions that have reached the state's courts and tribunals, and for the vehicle entry restrictions and registration requirements that some destinations have adopted. Hoteliers are divided. Those with established properties see managed limits as protection of the asset. Those building new capacity see the same instrument as a barrier written by incumbents.
What a longer season would take

Everyone in the bazaar agrees the answer is to lengthen the season, and nobody agrees on how. The proposals are familiar: promote the monsoon as a birdwatching and trekking window, develop winter sport where the snow is reliable, court the small-group corporate offsite market, and build enough conference space to justify a midweek booking in October.

Each of those requires something the town does not control. Off-season trekking needs marked and maintained routes and a rescue arrangement. Corporate business needs road reliability during the monsoon, which is a state highways question complicated by slope stability. Winter tourism needs the snow to arrive, which it has done less predictably in recent years, a point locals raise more often than any brochure does.
In the meantime the pattern holds. The rooms come down in price, the seasonal staff go home, the repairs begin, and the town spends the monsoon getting ready to make a year's income in four months.

title: The paper trail behind plastic recycling credits does not always lead to a recycler
dek: Obligated companies are buying certificates against waste that recyclers may never have processed, and the arithmetic of the market does not close.

body.text: The design of India's extended producer responsibility framework for plastics is straightforward. A company that puts packaging on the market incurs an obligation to have an equivalent quantity recycled or otherwise processed. Registered recyclers generate certificates when they process waste, obligated companies buy those certificates through the central portal, and the regulator can see, in principle, that the tonnes claimed match the tonnes processed.

The difficulty is that the framework verifies documents rather than material. A certificate is generated against a filing. The filing rests on records of waste purchased and processed, which rest in turn on invoices from aggregators and transporters in a trade that has operated in cash and on trust for decades.

Compliance managers at obligated companies, consultants who broker credits, and recyclers themselves describe a market where prices have moved in ways that the physical economics of recycling struggle to explain.
How a credit is created

A registered recycler declares an installed processing capacity when it enrols on the portal. It then reports quantities of waste procured and processed, supported by purchase records, weighbridge slips and, where applicable, electricity consumption consistent with running the plant. Certificates are issued against the processed quantity, categorised by the class of plastic, and are then available for transfer to an obligated entity.

Three of those inputs are difficult to falsify and one is not. Installed capacity can be inspected. Electricity consumption is metered by a third party. A weighbridge slip is a physical document. Purchase records from an informal aggregator, however, are generated by the recycler and the aggregator between themselves, and multiple people in the trade said that is where the quantity can be inflated.

The categories matter as much as the quantities. Certificates for rigid plastics, which have genuine scrap value and were being collected and recycled long before any regulation existed, are easier to substantiate than certificates for multilayer packaging, which has little scrap value and is the category the framework was principally designed to address.

"Nobody was paying to collect multilayer sachets from a village in Madhya Pradesh before this rule existed, and the collection network to do it did not appear in eighteen months," said a consultant who arranges compliance for consumer goods companies. "Yet the certificates for that category were available, and they were cheap."
The arithmetic that does not close

Two figures should broadly correspond: the volume of certificates issued in a category, and the volume of that material actually collected and processed. Where the second figure can be estimated from independent sources, waste characterisation studies, municipal collection data, the capacity and utilisation of processing plants, practitioners say the correspondence is poor for the low-value categories.

A second check is capacity. A plant's stated throughput implies a ceiling on what it can process in a year, and that ceiling can be compared with what it has claimed. Regulators have suspended registrations where the claim exceeded the plant's physical possibility, which establishes both that the problem exists and that it is detectable when someone looks.

The third check is the co-processing route, under which plastic waste is used as fuel in cement kilns. That pathway is capacity-constrained and well documented at the receiving end, which makes claims against it more verifiable and, correspondingly, more expensive to buy.
Why prices moved the way they did

Certificate prices in the early cycles rose sharply as obligated companies discovered that supply was thin. They then fell, in some categories steeply, in a period when neither collection infrastructure nor recycling capacity had expanded enough to explain the change. Buyers who had contracted at the higher level found themselves paying multiples of what the market was clearing at weeks later.

Compliance teams at larger companies responded by moving away from spot purchases towards direct arrangements: contracting with a named recycler, auditing the plant themselves, tracing material from a defined collection programme, and accepting a higher cost per tonne in exchange for a claim they can defend in a sustainability disclosure that carries its own liability.
That bifurcation is now the market's clearest feature. There is a documented, audited, expensive tonne and an undocumented, cheap one, and both discharge the same obligation on the portal.
What enforcement would actually need

The instruments largely exist. Registration can be suspended, environmental compensation can be levied, and the portal already holds the data required to run capacity and consistency checks across the whole registered base rather than one plant at a time.

What is scarce is inspection capacity at the state boards, which are responsible for physically verifying plants and are staffed for a range of duties of which this is one. Practitioners argue for automated screening, cross-referencing claimed throughput against installed capacity, electricity consumption and transport records, so that field inspection is directed at the outliers rather than distributed evenly across compliant and non-compliant operators.

Until that happens, the framework's central risk is not that companies evade the obligation. It is that they discharge it fully, at low cost, against tonnes of plastic that were never collected, and that the waste the rule was written about remains exactly where it was.

title: Bio-mining contracts promised to clear the dumps, and the dumps are still there
dek: Municipal remediation tenders assumed excavated waste would find buyers and land would be recovered. Neither assumption has held reliably.

body.text: Bio-mining is a simple idea applied to a difficult object. A legacy dumpsite, decades of mixed municipal waste piled into a hill, is excavated in lifts, screened into fractions, and disposed of by fraction: soil-like material back to the land or to horticulture, combustibles to a cement kiln or a waste-to-energy plant, recoverable metal and plastic to the scrap trade, and inert construction debris to fill.

Contracts on this model have been awarded by urban local bodies across the country, funded through central urban missions and state grants, and priced per tonne of legacy waste processed. Several have been completed and the reclaimed land handed back. Many others are running well behind schedule, and a number have been terminated or re-tendered.
The failures are not mysterious once the material flow is examined. The contracts pay for excavation and screening. They depend on somebody accepting what comes out.
What the contract actually buys

A per-tonne rate covers mobilisation of trommels and excavators, the labour to run them, fuel, dust suppression, leachate handling where required, and the contractor's margin. Rates are bid competitively and have been driven down in successive tenders, sometimes to a level that assumes the recovered fractions can be sold rather than paid to dispose of.

Where that assumption fails, the contractor's economics invert. Refuse-derived fuel from legacy waste is of poor and variable quality, with high moisture, chlorides and inert content, and cement plants that accept it do so selectively and at a gate fee rather than a purchase price, if they accept it at all. Transport to a kiln several hundred kilometres away can cost more than the processing itself.

The soil-like fraction is the larger problem by volume. It is typically the majority of what comes out of a legacy site, and its acceptability depends on contamination levels that vary through the pile. Where it cannot be applied to land, it must be placed somewhere, which usually means a scientific landfill cell that the city has not built.

"We bid the tonne, not the destination, and that was the industry's collective mistake," said a project head at a contractor that has run two legacy remediation sites in central India. "On paper the fractions have value. At the gate, half of them have a cost."
Where the excavated material goes

The most successful projects have been those where a destination was arranged before the excavator arrived: a cement plant within economic trucking distance with a contracted acceptance quantity, an approved use for the soil fraction in road embankment or mine reclamation, and a lined cell for the residue.

Where those arrangements were not in place, the pattern reported by municipal engineers is that the pile is not so much removed as rearranged. Screened material accumulates in stacks on the same site awaiting an offtake that does not materialise, and the reclaimed area is smaller than the completion certificate implies.

Monsoon compounds this. Excavation of an old dump exposes material that absorbs water, which stops screening entirely for weeks, generates leachate that the site's drainage was never designed to intercept, and produces odour complaints from neighbourhoods that in many cases grew up around the dumpsite after it was sited on what was then the edge of the city.
The rate that does not cover the work

Because tenders are awarded on lowest cost, bidders have an incentive to assume favourable material composition and a receptive market for the output. The site that is actually excavated frequently differs from the site described in the tender document, particularly in its inert and construction debris content, which affects both the screening rate and the disposal cost.

Payment terms then compound the problem. Contractors are paid against measured quantities certified by the urban local body, and municipal payment cycles are slow, which imposes a working capital burden on firms that are often mid-size and thinly capitalised. Several terminations have followed a familiar sequence: slower progress, disputed measurement, delayed payment, demobilised equipment.
What is being tried instead

Better-structured procurements have begun to price the destination rather than only the excavation. That means the tender specifies where each fraction will go, the urban local body commits to a disposal cell for the residue, and the payment schedule recognises that the soil-like fraction is a cost centre rather than a revenue line.

The other adjustment is upstream and less visible. A city that continues to send unsegregated mixed waste to a fresh dumping ground while bio-mining the old one is creating tomorrow's remediation contract with today's collection system. The municipalities most often cited as successful, including the ones that repeatedly top the national cleanliness rankings, are those that fixed segregation and processing first, and treated the legacy site as the closing item rather than the headline project.
That sequence is harder to fund, because a functioning collection system does not photograph as well as a hill being levelled, and it does not come with a completion date that fits a term of office.

title: In the dismantling lanes, formalisation arrives one licence at a time
dek: The informal trade still outbids authorised recyclers for old electronics, and the rules are only slowly changing who gets the material.

body.text: The lane is barely wide enough for a handcart. On either side, ground floor rooms open directly onto it, and in each one two or three people sit on the floor with screwdrivers, pliers and a plastic tub. A laptop takes about four minutes: battery out, screen separated, keyboard assembly aside, the board into the tub that matters, the plastic housing into the sack that does not.

Nobody in the lane calls this recycling. It is called kabaad ka kaam, scrap work, and it has been organised the same way for thirty years, through a chain of collectors, sorters, dismantlers and buyers who each take a defined step and a defined margin, with pricing settled daily by telephone against metal rates.

This is the system that authorised recyclers, holding consent from the state pollution control board and registration under the e-waste rules, have been trying to compete with since the rules were first framed.
The route a dead laptop takes

It usually begins with a household or a small office selling to a doorstep collector, or with a bulk consumer disposing of an ageing fleet through a tender. From there it passes to a local aggregator, then to a specialist who separates the categories that are worth separating, and then to the dismantlers whose only interest is what the board, the connectors and the wiring contain.

Each step adds a margin and each step is cash-settled. Nobody in the chain issues a document that would allow a producer to demonstrate compliance with a recycling obligation, and nobody in the chain has any incentive to start.

The final step is where the environmental problem sits. Extracting metal from boards profitably requires either a smelter with emission control or a chemical process with effluent treatment, and neither exists in a ground floor room. The methods available in the lane, acid leaching in open containers and burning of wire insulation to recover copper, are the ones that make e-waste a public health question rather than only a materials question.

"The dismantling in the lane is skilled work and it is not the problem," said an operations manager at an authorised recycler on the outskirts of the National Capital Region. "The problem is the last step, and that step happens because there is no legal buyer within reach paying a fair price for the board."
Why the formal sector cannot outbid the lane

An authorised facility carries costs the lane does not: consent fees, pollution control equipment, effluent handling, formal wages with statutory contributions, insurance, record keeping and the tax on every transaction. It also generally cannot recover the full metal value on site, because refining capacity for the precious metal fraction is limited domestically and boards are frequently exported for that step.

The lane carries none of those costs and can therefore pay more for the same laptop. Bulk consumers with a compliance requirement, listed companies, banks, government departments, will route material formally because their auditors ask. Households and small businesses sell to whoever is at the door with cash, and that is not the authorised recycler.

The regulatory response has been to make producers pay for the gap. Under the current framework, obligated producers buy recycling certificates from authorised recyclers, and the revenue from those certificates is what allows a formal facility to pay a competitive collection price. Floor pricing for those certificates has been introduced precisely because, without it, the transfer was too small to change the economics on the doorstep.
What a licence changes

A handful of operators in the informal trade have made the transition, generally with support from a producer, an industry programme or a development organisation. The transition is not a technology upgrade so much as an accounting one: a registered premises, a bank account through which material is bought, invoices, weighment records, wage registers and an audit trail that can support a certificate.

Those who have done it describe a business that is more stable and less profitable in the short run, and that becomes viable only with certificate revenue attached. The ones who have not point to the working capital required to buy material by bank transfer in a trade that has always paid cash on collection, which is a financing problem rather than an attitude problem.

The most durable arrangements have not tried to replace the collection network but to buy from it. A formal facility that purchases from lane aggregators, documents the transaction and performs only the hazardous steps itself keeps the informal sector's collection efficiency and moves the dangerous processing indoors, which is the outcome the rules are meant to produce.
The next material is already arriving

Lithium-ion batteries from phones, laptops and now two-wheelers are entering the same chain, and they behave very differently in a ground floor room. A punctured cell is a fire, and scrap markets have already recorded them. Battery waste rules place a recycling obligation on producers along similar lines to e-waste, and formal capacity for shredding cells and producing black mass has been built ahead of the volume.

Whether that material reaches the formal capacity will be decided by the same doorstep arithmetic that governs laptops. Recyclers say the difference this time is that the hazard is immediate and visible rather than chronic, and that a single warehouse fire changes how an insurer, a landlord and a municipal authority think about who is allowed to store what.

In the lane, the tubs are filling as they always have. The man sorting boards says the phone rates have been good this month, and asks whether the price for old batteries is going to be worth the trouble.

title: After the tap connections, the harder question of who pays to keep them running
dek: Village committees now own the schemes the state built, along with the power bills, pump failures and tariff collections that come with them.

body.text: The pipeline is the easy part. Across hundreds of villages in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, the household tap connections promised under the Jal Jeevan Mission have been laid, commissioned, photographed and reported up the chain. What follows is less photogenic. There is an electricity bill for the pumping station, a monthly payment for the operator who switches it on, a chlorination schedule that somebody has to maintain, and a household tariff that somebody else has to knock on doors to collect.

Responsibility for that arithmetic sits with the village water and sanitation committee, a sub-committee of the gram panchayat to which the state rural water supply department transfers the scheme once construction is certified complete. On paper the division of labour is settled: the state builds, the village runs. Engineers in three states described the handover as the point at which a significant share of schemes begin to drift, quietly, without any single moment of failure that anyone has to report.

The policy question has therefore shifted. It is no longer how many connections exist. It is whether a connection commissioned three summers ago is still delivering water this summer, and who is paying for it to do so.
A handover that assumes a treasurer

The standard operating model asks the committee to open a bank account, fix a tariff by resolution of the gram sabha, read meters where meters exist, bank the collections and pay the electricity board on time. Monthly household tariffs in the schemes described by officials for this article range from about fifty rupees to a little over a hundred and fifty. Collection efficiency is the number that nobody reports upward, and the one that determines everything else.

Where collections fall short, the gap is usually absorbed by the panchayat from its untied funds, including the tied grants for water and sanitation routed through the Fifteenth Finance Commission. That holds for a year or two. It stops holding when a submersible pump burns out and the replacement costs more than a quarter of the panchayat's annual water budget, or when the electricity connection has been sanctioned at a commercial tariff rather than the agricultural slab the village assumed it would get.

"We can collect from the households that get water at seven in the morning," said a panchayat secretary in Beed district. "The houses at the tail end of the line pay once, and then they stop, because for three weeks nothing came out of the tap."
Where the schemes fail first

Single-village schemes drawing from a borewell or an open well inside the revenue boundary are the ones a panchayat can plausibly run. Multi-village schemes are a different proposition. They involve intake works on a dam or a river, a treatment plant, pumping mains crossing several kilometres of undulating ground, and a bulk water charge payable to the source authority. Running one needs an electrical supervisor, a chemist and a maintenance contract, none of which a committee of eleven villagers is equipped to procure or supervise.

Source sustainability is the other early failure, and the less visible one. A scheme designed around a borewell yielding a comfortable discharge in a wet year is not the same scheme when the water table drops through a dry one. Recharge structures built with MGNREGA labour are meant to close that gap, but they are sanctioned by a different department, on a different calendar, and are rarely mapped to the specific aquifer feeding the specific scheme they are supposed to protect.

District officials describe a familiar sequence. The yield falls, supply hours are cut, the tail end of the network stops receiving water, collections from the tail end stop with it, and the committee then cannot pay the power bill that would have run the pump for longer hours.
The money after the money

Capital funding for the mission was always finite. Operations and maintenance were meant to come from user charges topped up by Finance Commission grants, with the state absorbing power costs in some places and not in others. Several states are now assembling a para-worker layer around that assumption: trained pump operators, village-level plumbers who can replace a valve without waiting for a block engineer, and self-help group members paid a small honorarium to run field test kits and log the results.

A second approach removes the work from the village altogether. A handful of districts have tendered cluster-level operations contracts under which a single operator maintains the schemes of twenty or thirty villages and is paid against functional connections rather than against assets built. That structure needs bulk metering at the source and at each village inlet, which most schemes still lack, and it needs a collection mechanism the operator can actually rely on rather than one that depends on the standing of a particular sarpanch.

"Performance contracts only work if somebody can measure performance," said a water sector consultant who has advised two state missions on operations funding. "If there is no meter at the inlet, you are paying a contractor for a promise."
What functionality actually measures

Functionality, in the mission's own definition, is not the existence of a tap. It is delivery of a prescribed quantity per person per day, at a regular frequency, of water meeting the drinking water standard. Third-party surveys apply that definition. District dashboards, in practice, are often populated from work completion certificates. The distance between those two numbers is where the argument about the programme's success will be conducted for the rest of the decade.

What the next phase requires is unglamorous. Energy audits of pumping stations, metering at the source, a repair supply chain for pumps and valves within a day's travel of every block, and a tariff that a sarpanch can defend in front of a gram sabha in a bad year. None of it produces a ribbon-cutting. All of it decides whether the taps that have already been counted are still running when the counting stops.

title: City utilities put treated sewage on the market, and industry starts signing for it
dek: Municipal reuse tenders are moving from pilot to contract, with polishing plants selling water to power stations, refineries and dyeing clusters.

body.text: Municipal corporations in Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Gujarat have floated or awarded a fresh round of tenders for tertiary treatment plants whose output is contracted to industrial buyers instead of being discharged into a drain. The structure is broadly the same in each case. The city supplies secondary treated sewage at a nominal charge, a concessionaire builds and operates a polishing plant, and an industrial off-taker signs a long-term agreement to lift an agreed volume every day whether or not it needs all of it.

The commercial logic runs in both directions. A utility converts a disposal liability into an annuity, and reduces the freshwater it is obliged to divert to industry from a reservoir that households also draw on. The buyer gets a supply that does not fail in April, does not depend on the monsoon arriving on schedule, and is not subject to the political risk that attaches to industrial allocations during a drought year.
What has changed is not the technology, which has been in service for more than a decade. It is the willingness of industrial buyers to sign take-or-pay commitments long enough to finance the plant.
The price that makes it work

Reuse water is priced below the industrial freshwater tariff, which in most states is set well above cost to cross-subsidise domestic connections. That spread is the entire business case. Concession agreements typically index the tariff to power costs, since pumping and reverse osmosis are the dominant operating expense, and increasingly to a chemicals index as well.

Distance decides viability more than anything else in the specification. Beyond roughly fifteen to twenty kilometres of transmission, depending on terrain and the number of lifts, the pumping cost erodes the discount that made the contract attractive. The transactions that have closed are the ones where a large industrial consumer sits close to a sewage treatment plant with reliable inflow, which is why the early deals cluster around refinery and power station belts rather than around the largest cities.

Capital structures lean on state support. Viability gap funding, urban mission grants and state reuse policies have covered part of the build cost in several projects, with concession periods of twenty to twenty-five years. Lenders have been more comfortable where the off-taker is a public sector undertaking than where it is a cluster of private units contracting individually.

"A lender is not underwriting a treatment plant, it is underwriting the off-take," said a project finance executive at an infrastructure lender in Mumbai. "One state-owned buyer on a twenty-year contract is worth more than forty textile units on annual renewals."
Where the volumes are

Sewage generation in Indian cities continues to run well ahead of installed treatment capacity, and a substantial share of the capacity that exists is not consistently loaded. Reuse projects are therefore competing for a subset of plants that already work. Several state reuse policies now direct industries located within a defined radius of a treatment plant to source a proportion of their requirement from it, which changes the negotiation from a sales pitch into a compliance discussion.

The specification the buyer needs varies more than the volume. Cooling tower makeup can tolerate parameters that boiler feed cannot, and demineralised water for a high-pressure boiler requires a further treatment stage the concessionaire may or may not be contracted to supply. Dyeing and processing clusters care about total dissolved solids and chlorides above all, because a shade variation caused by feed water is a rejected consignment.
The parts that break

Inlet quality is the risk that concessionaires price most carefully. Where industrial effluent enters the municipal sewer network, as it does in many older industrial towns, the biology at the secondary stage is periodically damaged, and the polishing plant downstream receives water it was not designed for. Contracts now specify inlet parameters and allocate the cost of deviation, but enforcement depends on the corporation policing its own network, which is a harder undertaking than operating a plant.

Reject management is the second constraint, and it is a physical one. A reverse osmosis stage produces a concentrated stream that has to go somewhere. Coastal cities can permit a marine outfall. Inland cities cannot, which leaves evaporation, deep injection or a further concentration step, each of which adds cost that the tariff has to absorb.

"Everybody plans for the permeate and nobody plans for the reject," said an operations head at a water treatment company that runs two municipal reuse plants. "In an inland city, the reject decides whether the project is buildable at all."
What the next round will test

Three questions remain open. Whether municipal counterparties pay on time without a state-backed escrow. Whether industries in sectors with strict process water requirements, notably food processing and pharmaceuticals, will accept reuse water for anything beyond utilities and cooling. And whether groundwater regulation tightens enough in stressed blocks that reuse becomes the cheapest route to compliance rather than a reputational purchase.

Officials handling the current tenders expect the answer to the third question to arrive first. Where abstraction approvals for industry have become slower and conditional, procurement teams that previously treated reuse as a corporate sustainability line item have begun evaluating it as a security-of-supply decision, which is a different conversation with a different budget behind it.

title: On Bengaluru's eastern corridor, the water arrives by truck and the price moves by the week
dek: Borewell filling points, apartment associations and a few hundred tanker operators run a parallel utility for the city's IT belt.

body.text: The queue forms before six in the morning on a service road off Varthur, at a filling point that looks like nothing at all: a compound wall, a gate, a borewell head, and a length of hose thick enough to fill a six thousand litre tanker in under twenty minutes. By seven, fourteen trucks have come and gone. The operator at the gate keeps count in a notebook, one line per load, and settles with the landowner at the end of the week.

This is the supply system that keeps a substantial part of Bengaluru's eastern corridor functioning. The apartment towers of Whitefield, Sarjapur Road, Panathur and Varthur went up faster than the piped network reached them, and many were commissioned on the assumption that borewells inside the compound plus tankers from outside would cover the difference until the next stage of the Cauvery scheme arrived.
For a decade, that assumption worked well enough to be invisible. Then a dry year arrived, the in-compound borewells began yielding air, and the parallel utility became the only utility.
The economics of a load

A tanker operator's cost sheet is short. Diesel, driver wages, the payment to the filling point per load, tyres, and the instalment on the truck. The price charged to a customer moves with none of those inputs directly. It moves with how far the tanker has to travel to find a borewell that is still yielding, and how many households are calling that morning.

In a normal month, the same six thousand litre load might change hands at a price that a housing society treats as a routine line item. In a bad March, when the nearest filling points have gone dry and trucks are driving out towards the district boundary to load, the price climbs steeply, waiting times stretch from two hours to most of a day, and societies start rationing supply to a few hours each morning and evening.

Facility managers describe the same defensive playbook. Book earlier, book from more than one operator, keep the sump full rather than running it down, and start metering flats individually so that consumption falls when the price rises.

"Once we billed water per flat instead of splitting it across maintenance, consumption dropped by close to a fifth within two months," said the general secretary of an apartment owners association off Sarjapur Road. "Nobody installed anything. People simply stopped running the tap while brushing."
Where the water actually comes from

Most filling points are private borewells on land that was agricultural until recently, at the fringe of the built-up area, in Anekal, Sarjapur, Devanahalli and along the road out towards Hoskote. The economics for the landowner are simple. A borewell that once irrigated a few acres of ragi or mulberry now sells its output by the tanker load, at a return per litre that no crop in the district can approach.

The depths tell the rest of the story. Wells that were drilled to a few hundred feet a generation ago are now routinely sunk past a thousand, and in parts of the corridor beyond that, into hard rock where yields depend on intersecting a fracture rather than reaching a water table. Rigs are booked weeks ahead through the dry months. A dry bore still costs the owner the full drilling charge.

Hydrogeologists have pointed out for years that the corridor is drawing from a system that recharges slowly and is being pumped by thousands of independent users with no shared meter between them. The lake network that once did the recharging has been built over in places, encroached in others, and in several cases receives untreated sewage that makes the shallow aquifer beneath it unusable for drinking in any case.
After the crisis, the rules

The city's response to the last acute shortage was administrative. Tanker operators were required to register with the district administration, a ceiling was announced for what could be charged per load by distance slab, and the water board pressed ahead with extending the Cauvery network to the outer wards that had been outside it since municipal boundaries were expanded.

Enforcement of the price ceiling was uneven, as operators and residents both acknowledge. Registration did produce something more durable, which is a rough count of how many trucks are running and from where they load. Alongside it came a stronger push on demand: mandatory rainwater harvesting for larger plots, penalties for using potable water to wash cars and water gardens, and a requirement that large apartment complexes run their own sewage treatment plants and reuse the output through a second set of pipes for flushing and landscaping.

Dual plumbing has become the visible dividing line between buildings commissioned recently and those that were not. Where it exists, a treatment plant that works well can cut the volume a society has to buy in by a meaningful share. Where the plant is badly run, and many are, residents complain about odour and the association quietly goes back to buying tankers.

"We are asked to keep a plant running to a standard the city does not meet in its own network," said a facility manager responsible for three complexes in Whitefield. "When it works, we buy fewer loads. When the operator changes, everything has to be relearned."
A utility nobody planned

Piped supply is arriving in the corridor, ward by ward, and connection drives have begun in areas that never had a municipal meter. That will change the arithmetic of the tanker market without ending it. Construction sites will keep buying by the load. Buildings will keep tankers on standby for the weeks when the pipeline is under maintenance. Filling points on the fringe will keep selling, because the demand is close and the alternative is a crop.

What the corridor has built, in the absence of a plan, is a functioning market with no meter at the source, no record of how much is being withdrawn, and a price signal that only appears once the shortage has already arrived. It moves water reliably. It says nothing at all about how much is left.
